This page documents every variable in `class_data_raw.csv`. Variable names, types, and one-line
descriptions come from the course's official `codebook.xlsx` (also available in `data_raw/`);
background and methodology for the tract-level environmental measures is pulled in from
`Classdata_arealevelmeasures_description.docx`. It's meant as a reference to check back to while
working through the lessons — you don't need to read it top to bottom.

::: {.callout-tip}
## About this dataset

The primary class dataset is based on the **Southeast Pennsylvania Household Survey** and
represents a **simulated** cross-sectional survey of adults living in Philadelphia in 2015
(participants identified via random-digit dialing in the scenario the data represent). It's
fictitious data designed to resemble real-world data, not actual study participants — this lets
you work through realistic epidemiologic problems without using identifiable data.

`class_data_raw.csv` contains **2,000 observations and 38 variables**: health outcomes, health
behaviors, demographic/socioeconomic characteristics, perceptions of neighborhood conditions, and
geographic location. `PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv` (384 Philadelphia census tracts) is a separate
file you'll link in during Lesson 1.
:::

## Individual-Level Variables

### Identifiers & Geography

| Variable | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | Integer | Random identification number |
| `geoid10` | String | 2010 Census tract identifier (GEOID) — used to link to tract-level data |
| `year` | Integer | Year when data are collected |

### Demographics & Socioeconomic Status

| Variable | Type | Description |

| `gender` | String | Gender identity ('Woman', 'Man', 'Non-binary') |
| `race_ethnicity` | String | Race/ethnicity of the individual (e.g., 'Black', 'White', 'Hispanic', 'Other') |

## Area-Level (Tract-Level) Variables

These variables describe the census tract (`geoid10`) each participant lives in, rather than the
participant individually — everyone living in the same tract shares the same value.

### Population Density

| Variable | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `popden_km` | Numeric | Population density in the census tract (people per km²) |

### Traffic Volume

**Variable:** `ctb1traff` (Numeric — "Traffic density" per the official codebook)

Measured and estimated traffic volumes for major roads by road section are available annually
from PennDOT (2005–present). Air pollution levels from traffic typically return to background
levels within 100 to 300 m of roads. We calculated kernel densities of average daily traffic from
PennDOT traffic data within 100 m and 300 m of road centerlines, on a 30 m grid, for southeastern
Pennsylvania.

- 100 m was chosen based on work done for the New York City Community Air Survey.
- 300 m was chosen to account for the road width of wider roads.

The variable in the data set represents the **average of the 100 m kernel-density average daily
traffic** in the participant's residential census tract. **Higher value = greater traffic
volume.**

**Data sources**

- *Background:* Annual Average Daily Traffic by road segment, from the Pennsylvania Department of
  Transportation (PennDOT), Bureau of Planning and Research, Geographic Information Division.
- *Data obtained:* Downloaded from [www.pasda.psu.edu](http://www.pasda.psu.edu) (2005–2015
  downloaded 11/4/2016; 2016–2017 downloaded 4/26/2017).

### Land Cover: Tree Canopy & Grass/Shrub Cover

| Variable | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `hrlctree` | Numeric | Tree canopy cover (proportion in the census tract) |
| `hrlcgrass_shrub` | Numeric | Grass or shrub cover (proportion in the census tract) |

Derived from the Philadelphia Land Cover Raster, which provides data on surface types in
Philadelphia in 2008 and an update in 2018 (the 2015 value in this data set was created using
linear interpolation between the two). The data identifies seven categories: tree canopy,
grass/shrub, bare earth, water, buildings, roads, and other paved surfaces. When tree canopy
covers another surface type, that area is placed in the tree canopy category. Data were gathered
with the assistance of the University of Vermont Spatial Analysis Laboratory.

You can calculate a total vegetation measure by summing `hrlctree` and `hrlcgrass_shrub` together.

### Tract-Level Sociodemographic Composition

| Variable | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `race_blackNH` | Numeric | Proportion non-Hispanic Black residents in the census tract |
| `race_whiteNH` | Numeric | Proportion non-Hispanic White residents in the census tract |
| `race_hisp` | Numeric | Proportion Hispanic residents in the census tract |
| `Educ_ltHS` | Numeric | Proportion of tract residents with less than a high school education |
| `Educ_ltba` | Numeric | Proportion of tract residents with less than a bachelor's degree |
| `pov_allage` | Numeric | Proportion of tract residents living in poverty |
| `unemployed` | Numeric | Proportion of tract unemployed |

**Data sources**

- *Background:* The American Community Survey (ACS), administered by the U.S. Census Bureau, is a
  nationwide survey providing social, economic, housing, and demographic data. The Census Bureau
  combines five consecutive years to produce estimates at the census tract level.
- *Data obtained:* ACS 5-year average data for 2017–2021, downloaded from the U.S. Census Bureau.
  Race/ethnicity variables were calculated as the percentage of persons in the census tract
  identifying with each category, across all age/gender groups. **Data may be missing** if a
  measure was suppressed by the Census Bureau due to low sample size (to protect against
  potentially identifying information).

### Crime Variables

| Variable | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ctviolra` | Numeric | Violent crime rate — units unconfirmed, see flag below |
| `ctviolkm` | Numeric | Violent crime rate per km² in the census tract |

Police-reported crime data is available from OpenDataPhilly. Yearly crime **rates** and
**densities** (per square mile/km) for the City of Philadelphia were created for calendar years
2006–2016. Crimes are categorized, with rates/densities available for violent crime, narcotic
drug violations, and property crime, summarized by 2010 U.S. Census Tract. These rates were
generated to provide objective measures of neighborhood safety, and can be used to explore the
influence of crime and safety on health outcomes and behaviors.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Unresolved: units for `ctviolra`

Two source documents disagree on the unit for `ctviolra`, and this hasn't been confirmed yet:

- `Classdata_arealevelmeasures_description.docx` describes it as a rate **per 10,000 population**.
- The official `codebook.xlsx` (and the `create_data.R` script that generated it) describes it as
  **"Total violent crime incidents per 1,000 residents."**

Leaving this unresolved for now, per instructor note — don't state a specific unit for
`ctviolra` in student-facing material until this is confirmed.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
The source `.docx` also lists a missing-data sentinel value of `9999999999` for the crime
variables. That value does **not** actually appear anywhere in `class_data_raw.csv` (checked
directly) — it looks like a leftover description from the original real-data source system, not
something present in this simulated class dataset. No special recoding is needed for
`ctviolra`/`ctviolkm` on that account.
:::

## Known Missingness in This Dataset

A few variables have a small number of true `NA` values, deliberately built into the simulated
data set (confirmed by counting missing values directly in `class_data_raw.csv`):

| Variable | # Missing (of 2,000) |
|---|---|
| `mental_health` | 42 |
| `current_smoker` | 20 |
| `high_blood_pressure` | 12 |
| `stress` | 7 |
| `has_park` | 5 |
| `age` | 3 |
| `gender` | 2 |

All other variables are complete.

## Known Data Quirks

- **`age` has 4 implausible outliers** coded as 116 years old. These are intentional (built into
  the simulated data for teaching purposes) — an example of the kind of value that should catch
  your eye during exploratory data analysis (e.g., via `summary()` or a histogram), well before
  any modeling. You'll work through recoding this in the Exploratory Data Analysis lesson.
